segments.say: It's a calm evening in the new flat, a couple of weeks in. Ines has unpacked three more boxes, and she's sitting on the edge of her bed with a cup of tea, thinking about her hand and the light switch. It's still a small mystery to her. How does a hand learn something so thoroughly that it keeps doing it without her? Somewhere in her head, she imagines, there must be a place where this kind of knowing lives. And there is, in a way.

So let's take a gentle look at what's going on inside, and we'll keep it simple, because nobody needs a diagram of the brain at this hour. Please treat what follows as a friendly sketch rather than a full map. The brain is wonderfully complicated, and scientists are still working out a lot of it. But a few broad ideas have held up well over many years of research, and those ideas turn out to be easy to picture.

The first idea is one we met a little earlier. Researchers often describe two ways our actions can be controlled. In one, we act because we know what we want, and we expect a certain action to get it. That's goal-directed control. In the other, we act because a familiar cue has set off a familiar response. That's habitual control. And a recurring question in neuroscience is where each of these lives, and how an action moves from one to the other.

It might help to hold three small thoughts together. Goal-directed control is aimed at an outcome. You do something because of what it will bring. Habitual control is set off by a cue, and it runs more or less on its own. And the third thought is the interesting one. With enough repetition, an action that began as goal-directed can slowly become habitual. The very same movement, but now steered from a different place.

show.title: Two ways of steering
items: Habitual: set off by a cue

segments.say: Two regions sitting side by side deep in the brain turn out to have different jobs. One is important for goal-directed actions, and the other for habits. That was a main conclusion of a review by Henry Yin and Barbara Knowlton, published in 2006, in the journal Nature Reviews Neuroscience. It was called The Role of the Basal Ganglia in Habit Formation. They pulled together animal research on how goal-directed actions are transformed into habitual responses, and what happens in the brain as that change takes place.

show.what: Two neighbouring brain regions, one for goals, one for habits

segments.say: The basal ganglia are a group of structures tucked deep inside the brain, below the wrinkled outer surface. They're connected to movement, to learning, and to the way we pick up routines. Inside them is a region called the striatum, and the striatum has different areas that do different things. You don't need to remember the names tonight. But it's rather lovely to know that the quiet machinery of habit has a real address, somewhere warm and well hidden inside the head.

show.sub: A group of structures deep inside

segments.say: Yin and Knowlton describe two of those neighbouring areas. The dorsomedial striatum, which they call the associative area, turns out to be crucial for goal-directed actions. And the dorsolateral striatum, which they call the sensorimotor area, turns out to be crucial for stimulus-driven habits. Medial means toward the middle, and lateral means toward the side. So, one area leans in toward the middle, and the other sits a little further out. Two neighbours, with two different jobs.

Now here's the heart of it. According to the review, habit formation corresponds to a shift of control. The authors describe it as a shift from one network to the other, from the associative network linked to goals, toward the sensorimotor network linked to habits. In simple terms, as an action is practiced again and again, the work of steering it moves, little by little, from a part of the brain that weighs goals toward a part that just runs the routine.

Picture it as a long, smooth curve. At the very beginning, a new action needs plenty of attention, and goals are firmly in charge. With every repetition, a little more of the steering is passed along. Then, after a good while, the routine is largely carried by the habit system, and it runs without much help. This is only an illustration of the idea, not a measurement. But it's a good picture of how a clumsy first attempt becomes something you do without thinking.

It's worth noticing what this handover is not. It isn't a moment where a switch is flipped. There's no morning when Ines wakes up and her brain announces that the light switch has now officially become a habit. It happens quietly, across many repetitions, in the background of ordinary days. And just like the path across a field, it's only afterward, when we glance back, that we see how deeply the track has been worn.

Here's a picture to hold on to. A narrow path across a hillside, pressed into the grass by countless footsteps. Nobody planned it. Nobody drew it on a map. It simply appeared, because many people walked the same way, one after another. That's a pretty good picture of a habit in the brain. Repetition wears a groove, and the groove makes the next trip a little easier, and the easier trip makes the groove a little deeper.

show.cap: A path worn by many footsteps

segments.say: You might wonder why the brain would bother with this arrangement at all. Why hand anything over? It seems like it would be simpler to have goals in charge of everything. But a moment's thought shows why it isn't. If every single movement needed careful weighing, we'd get through the day very slowly, and with very little attention left over. The handover isn't a flaw in the design. In a lot of ways, it is the design.

show.title: Why is it built this way?

segments.say: Think about tying your shoes. Once, it was a puzzle that took your full concentration, with your tongue sticking out. Now your fingers do it while you talk, or think about lunch. Or think about driving a road you know well. Your hands and feet do their jobs while your mind wanders. We can be very glad of that. Imagine having to relearn, from scratch, how to turn a key, every morning of your life.

It's quite a list, once you start. Tying laces. Typing a message. Driving a familiar road. Brushing your teeth. And, for Ines at least, finding the light switch in her old flat, in the dark, without a single thought. All of these were once effortful, and all of them have been quietly handed over. We tend not to thank our habit system, because it works so smoothly that we hardly notice it. But it deserves a small, warm thank you.

show.title: Quiet skills we're grateful for
items: Finding the right switch, in the right flat

segments.say: Yin and Knowlton also point to something a little humbling. Some of this kind of learning can happen without our awareness. Habit learning in people can proceed without us noticing it. That fits what Ines has found. She never sat down and decided to reach for her phone whenever she lay in bed. It was learned in the background, bit by bit, while she was busy with other things, like most of what we learn.

Yet there's the gentle catch, and we'll come back to it soon. Once an action has been handed over, it becomes stimulus-driven. That means it's set off by the cue, and it's no longer steered by a fresh look at what the action will bring. So a routine can keep going even after the reason for it has faded. That might sound odd, even a little worrying. But as we'll see, it's an ordinary result of a very useful design.

show.sub: When the routine outlasts the reason

segments.say: It's worth saying that one more time, slowly. The routine can outlast the reason. Ines has no reason left to reach for the old wall. And a habit that was once a good solution can stay on long after the question has changed. Nothing is broken when that happens. It's simply the habit system doing what it does, faithfully and without complaint, for a person who has moved on.

In the little flat, Ines has finished her tea, though it's gone cold. She smiles, picturing the quiet two neighbours deep in her head, one weighing goals, and one running routines. She isn't worried by any of it. There's something oddly comforting in knowing that her hand isn't being stubborn, only faithful to what it learned. And there's nothing she has to fix tonight. If anything, she feels a bit fond of her own hand. Tomorrow, she'll walk to the new office the long way, just to see it. For now, she turns the lamp off, on the right, on the first try.
